docs.title: deployforge
docs.text:
Ship Go apps to your own servers: release archives, not containers.

deployforge deploys Go web apps to hosts you already have. Each app is a single binary with a YAML config, run by systemd behind Caddy, with its secrets in a parameter store. A deploy builds a release from a clean, tagged commit, ships it with the app's config and secrets, runs the app's validate and migrate, switches to it, checks readiness, and restores the previous release on any failure, recording every release in a ledger.

Your repository keeps the configuration; deployforge is the binary.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Area What you get Guide The fleet document Hosts, apps and their named stacks as JSON, validated before anything runs The Fleet Document Deploys Releases from a clean, tagged commit; an atomic switch, readiness on every host name, automatic restore, a deploy lock, an audit log and a ledger; hooks Deploying Hosts systemd units with a sandbox and limits, an idempotent host-setup script, a Caddyfile per host Hosts The edge Cloudflare zones checked against their name servers, a security baseline, origin certificates made on the host, a TLS minimum check The Edge Databases Owner and app roles with connection limits and SCRAM verifiers, snapshots, copies between servers Databases Credentials The credential registry the fleet names: checked, generated, installed and set up step by step; a check before every deploy; IAM per stack Credentials Taking over Moving a stack another tool deployed, without a redeploy Taking Over a Stack Embedding Every capability as a Go package, and the command tree mountable in your own tool Embedding deployforge

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go install github.com/plexusone/deployforge/cmd/deployforge@latest

Then follow Getting Started.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
This guide covers how a fleet describes its credentials, the credentials commands that check, report on, generate, install and record them, the check deploy ship runs before packaging, and the iam command that gives each stack's parameter-store prefix its own IAM policy. The registry is in systemspec-credential format, and the commands run through credforge. For the fleet fields, see Fleet document. For the deploy that uses the check, see Deploying.

No command here prints a secret value. Checks read names, not values.

docs.title: The credentials section
docs.text:
The fleet document names the registry and the files beside it:

{
  "credentials": {
    "registry": "credentials/registry.json",
    "events": "credentials/events.json",
    "reviews": "credentials/reviews.json",
    "targets": "credentials/targets.json"
  }
}
  • registry: required. The credential registry file.
  • events: the event log. events.json beside the registry when empty.
  • reviews: review decisions. reviews.json beside the registry when empty.
  • targets: a credforge targets file that says how each store is reached. Without it, GitHub Actions secrets are reached with GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN, and SSM with the default AWS configuration. Either way, every app's repository is scanned.

Paths are relative to the fleet document. The credentials commands take --events to name another event log; the default is events.json.

Print the JSON Schema of the registry or the event log:

deployforge credentials schema registry
deployforge credentials schema events

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
deployforge credentials validate

validate fails on a registry or event log that is invalid. It then prints advice about entries that are valid but likely to mislead whoever sets them up. --strict fails on advice too.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
deployforge credentials status --system example-app --env prod

status lists every credential whose state is not ok, planned or retired, most urgent first. It exits non-zero when a listed credential is in a --fail-on state, so scripts and CI can use it as a gate. The default is expired,overdue.

Flags: --all, --as-of <date>, --env, --system, --manual, --progress <to-create,to-record,to-deploy,deployed,retired>, --state, and --warn-days (default 30).

docs.title: Record an event
docs.text:
deployforge credentials record 'example-app/prod/*' deployed --by operator

record <credential-id-or-pattern> <event> adds an event to the log. The event is one of created, rotated, expires, deployed, verified or revoked. In a pattern, * matches any text, slashes included. Flags: --at (a date or RFC 3339 time; default now), --by, --note, and --expires (required for expires, optional for created and rotated).

docs.title: Check the stores
docs.text:
deployforge credentials check --fail-on missing,stale,unregistered

check lists the names in every store the targets file reaches, never their values, and the secrets the scanned repositories' workflows read. It compares them with the registry and the event log. The states, most urgent first:

  • missing: a listed store does not hold the credential.
  • stale: a store was set before the current value was made.
  • unregistered: a workflow reads a secret the registry stores nowhere it can be read.
  • changed: a store was set after the log's latest event, and nothing was recorded.
  • unrecorded: a store holds a credential the log has no event for.
  • unlisted: a store holds a name no credential in use names.
  • unobserved: no binding reaches the store.
  • present: as recorded.

The exit status is 1 when a finding is in a --fail-on state (default missing,stale,unregistered), and 2 on an error. --record logs unrecorded stores as created and changed ones as deployed.

Other flags: --all, --format (text or json), --grace (default 24h), --include-planned, and --only <pattern>, such as 'example-app/prod/*'.

docs.title: Generate
docs.text:
deployforge credentials generate --dry-run
deployforge credentials generate --only 'example-app/prod/*'

generate makes each credential whose generation.format is set and whose provisioner is credforge generate or none. A format is a random value (hex32, base64url32) or a private key (p256-pem, ed25519-pem, rsa3072-pem). It writes the value to every primary store and records a created event. It never prints a value.

It makes a credential only when none of its primary stores holds a value, and writes a parameter only if the parameter still does not exist, so it never replaces a value. It lists what it will make and asks first. Flags: --dry-run, --yes, --by, --include-planned, --only.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
deployforge credentials install example-app/prod/api-token --expires 2027-01-31

install <credential> sets one credential's value in each store the registry lists for it that the targets file reaches: GitHub Actions secrets and SSM SecureString parameters. It lists the writes and asks before reading the value. The value is read once, hidden, from the terminal, or from standard input with --stdin and --yes. It is never an argument, never written to disk, and never printed.

Before it writes, it checks the value: a GitHub token must read each repository its entitlements name. Then it records a created event (rotated when the log has one) with the expiry, and a verified event for the checks that passed. A credential whose provisioner stores it is refused; run its command instead.

Flags: --dry-run, --yes, --stdin, --no-probe (write without checking first), --expires (YYYY-MM-DD or RFC 3339), --by.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
deployforge credentials report -f html -o credentials.html
deployforge credentials report -f plan --environment-order prod,staging -o plan.md

report writes one of five formats with -f:

  • html: one self-contained page to search and filter. This is the default.
  • markdown: a reference for documentation, from the registry only.
  • plan: the management plan: summary, launch checklist, rotation calendar, protections, exposure.
  • ics: the rotation calendar as an iCalendar file.
  • json: the rows with their state, for other tools.

Flags: -o, --title, --as-of, --warn-days, --months (calendar span; default 12), --remind-days, --environment-order, --system-order.

credentials export [-o file] writes the registry as JSON.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
deployforge credentials review

review serves a local page, on 127.0.0.1:8484 unless --addr says otherwise. It lists every credential with its stores, consumers, rotation and events. You record decisions (approved, change, remove) in the reviews file, and events in the event log. The registry is never written, and no value is read or shown. A live check from the page needs a targets file.

docs.title: Set up a system
docs.text:
deployforge credentials setup --system example-app --env prod list
deployforge credentials setup --system example-app --env prod run <step>
deployforge credentials setup --system example-app --env prod verify --all

setup builds a runbook from the registry for one system's credentials: what is set up at issuers, what tools make, and what a person gets from an issuer and installs, in order. Its subcommands are list, show, run, verify, record, validate, doc, export and schema. Each step is checked with credforge, which reads names and never values. Progress is kept in its own log beside the event log, such as setup-example-app-prod.json, unless --progress names another.

Common flags: --system, --env, --need (launch, later, optional; default launch), --progress, --root.

run refuses a step whose dependencies are not done unless you pass --force. It asks before each command unless you pass --yes, and runs commands without a shell. Give variables with --var name=<value>.

docs.title: Page for one stack
docs.text:
deployforge credentials page example-app prod -o example-app-prod.html

page <app> <stack> writes an HTML page of the credentials the stack needs, how each is made, where it is stored, whether the log records it, and the setup runbook. It holds no value. --need picks the needs to show; the default is launch,later,optional.

docs.title: Preflight for one stack
docs.text:
deployforge credentials preflight example-app prod
deployforge credentials preflight example-app prod --record

preflight <app> <stack> lists the stack's secret prefix and compares it with every active credential the registry stores there, as the check in deploy ship does, reading no value. It shows:

  • each credential present, with when its store last set it, and whether the event log records it;
  • each credential missing. One that is optional, by tag or by need, or needed only while another rotates (need: rotation), is never missing;
  • each name under the prefix no credential lists. A database move's values under next/ and previous/ are counted, not listed.

Flags:

  • --record: record each present credential the log lacks as created, at its store's time.
  • --include-planned: compare planned credentials too, such as those of a stack not yet deployed.
  • --require-recorded: exit non-zero while a present credential is unrecorded.

It exits non-zero when a credential is missing.

docs.title: The pre-flight in ship
docs.text: When the fleet document has a credentials section, deploy ship checks that every secret the registry stores under the stack's prefix is in the parameter store, by name, before it packages anything. A missing secret stops the deploy. Skip the check with --no-preflight.

docs.title: IAM for each stack
docs.text:
deployforge iam plan
deployforge iam policy example-app prod --account 123456789012
deployforge iam apply example-app prod --confirm
deployforge iam verify

iam <plan|apply|verify|policy> [<app> <stack>]... makes, for each named stack or every live one:

  • a policy ssm-<app>-<stack> that reads and writes the SSM parameters under the stack's secret prefix and lists parameter names;
  • a group <app>-<stack>-operators with the policy attached.

Group members are reported, never changed. plan lists what is missing, apply creates it and checks again, and verify fails unless everything is in place. Nothing is deleted.

apply changes the account's IAM, so it needs --confirm: without it, it shows the plan, changes nothing, and says to run again with --confirm. policy prints one stack's policy document for review, with --account naming the account the document is for; it reads no AWS account.

Flags:

  • --path: the IAM path of the policies and groups. Default /deployforge/.
  • --account: refuse to act unless the AWS profile is this account; with policy, the account the document names.
  • --confirm: with apply, make the changes the plan shows.
  • --region: the region of the parameters. Default $AWS_REGION.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
This guide covers the PostgreSQL side of a fleet: provisioning each stack's databases and roles, taking a snapshot of the database server, and moving a stack's databases to another server. It assumes the databaseServer section and each stack's databases in the Fleet document. deploy ship takes a snapshot for you before a primary stack; see Deploying. Connection strings are parameters in the stack's secret prefix; see Credentials.

All db commands take <app> <stack> and read the fleet document. psql runs on the via host, with the administrator's password on its standard input, so your machine need not reach the server.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
deployforge db roles plan example-app prod
deployforge db roles apply example-app prod --confirm
deployforge db roles verify example-app prod

roles provisions each database of a stack with:

  • an owner role, <db>_owner, which migrates the database;
  • an app role, <db>_app, when the database sets appRole, with rows only;
  • the stack's connectionLimit and statement and idle-in-transaction timeouts, on the role the app runs as;
  • CONNECT for the stack's own roles only.

Each role's password is kept in the stack's parameters. deployforge reuses a password that is there, makes and stores one that is not, and sends it to the server only as a SCRAM verifier.

The commands:

  • plan shows the parameters it would create or reuse, and the SQL, without passwords. It changes nothing.
  • apply --confirm creates the missing parameters, provisions the databases and roles, then verifies. It needs --confirm.
  • verify checks the server against the plan and exits non-zero on any difference. It reads no app's secret.

All three take --ssh-key for the via host.

docs.title: Staging for a stack that runs elsewhere
docs.text: A stack with status elsewhere keeps its live parameters until it moves. Its new values wait under <prefix>next/, which a deploy never reads. The move sequence below uses them.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text:
deploy ship takes a snapshot before the primary stack of an app with databases. You can take one by hand before a deploy whose migrate changes a schema. This applies when databaseServer.lightsailName is set.

deployforge db snapshot plan example-app prod --label v1.2.0
deployforge db snapshot apply example-app prod --label v1.2.0 --confirm
deployforge db snapshot list
deployforge db snapshot verify <snapshot>
  • plan shows the server, its state, the snapshot apply would take and the recent ones.
  • apply --confirm takes a manual snapshot and waits until it is available. --timeout sets how long to wait; the default is 30 minutes.
  • list lists the server's manual snapshots, newest first.
  • verify <snapshot> exits non-zero unless the snapshot is available.

A server holds every app's databases, so the snapshot does too. The app, the stack and --label name it and are kept as tags. deployforge deletes nothing: remove old snapshots in the Lightsail console, since each is billed for its storage.

docs.title: Copy a stack to another server
docs.text:
db copy reads each database's owner connection under --from and --to, each one of live, next or previous under the stack's secret prefix. It runs pg_dump | psql on the via host, in one transaction that first drops what the target's owner has. No owners or grants come from the source, so the target ends with exactly the source's objects, all owned by its owner. The connections stay in memory and reach the host on ssh's standard input.

deployforge db copy run example-app prod --from live --to next --confirm
deployforge db copy verify example-app prod --from live --to next
deployforge db copy promote example-app prod --confirm
  • run --confirm copies each database from --from to --to, replacing what the target has, then compares row counts.
  • verify compares each database's tables and exact row counts, and exits non-zero on any difference.
  • promote --confirm checks that every staged parameter exists, keeps each live one under previous/ (unless one is there already), and replaces it with its staged value. Deploys then use the new server.

Flags on all three: --from (default live), --to (default next), --skip <database> to leave a database for the app's migrate to build (repeat for each), and --ssh-key.

docs.title: Moving a stack
docs.text:
1. Run db roles apply --confirm. It makes the new server's roles and keeps their parameters under next/.
  2. Run db copy run --from live --to next --confirm.
  3. Run db copy promote --confirm.
  4. Set the stack's status to live in the fleet document, and deploy.
  5. For writes made on the old server meanwhile, run db copy run --from previous --to live --confirm.
deployforge db roles apply example-app prod --confirm
deployforge db copy run example-app prod --from live --to next --confirm
deployforge db copy promote example-app prod --confirm
deployforge deploy ship example-app prod --tag v1.2.0
deployforge db copy run example-app prod --from previous --to live --confirm

docs.title: Import a data-only dump
docs.text:
deployforge db import example-app prod app --file app-data.sql \
  --replace org-local=org-1234 --replace http://app.localhost:8080=https://app.example.com
deployforge db import example-app prod app --file app-data.sql --replace org-local=org-1234 --confirm

db import <app> <stack> <database> --file <dump> loads a plain data-only dump (pg_dump --data-only) into one of the stack's databases, such as the data a local copy of the app holds, once the stack's schema is in place:

  • It runs as the database's owner, with psql on the database server's via host, in one transaction. The owner's connection reaches the host on ssh's standard input.
  • Tables whose row-level security is forced on their owner have FORCE lifted for the load and put back in the same transaction.
  • It prints each table's row count after the load. Without --confirm the transaction is rolled back, so the counts show what the load would give and nothing changes.
  • A row whose key the database already has fails the whole load.
  • --replace OLD=NEW replaces text throughout the dump first, such as an ID that differs between the source and the stack, or a local host name. Repeat it for each.
  • The dump may hold no psql meta-command outside COPY data; pg_dump's \restrict and \unrestrict lines are dropped.

A tool embedding deployforge can add its own flags and replacements with Options.ImportHook. See Embedding.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text: This guide covers deploying a release to a stack, rolling it back, clearing a stale lock, reading status, what runs on the host, migrations a rollback can survive, reports for scripts and agents, the deploy ledger, hooks, and packaging a release archive. For a first deploy, see Getting started. To move a stack from another tool, see Taking over a stack. For the fields these commands read, see Fleet document.

docs.title: How a deploy runs
docs.text:
The operator's machine does the work that needs credentials: it reads the fleet document and the parameter store, and builds the release. It copies a linux/amd64 build of deployforge and the archive to the host, then runs deployforge there as root over SSH. There is no agent on the host.

Hosts are reached as <sshUser>@<address> with your system's ssh and scp, so your SSH configuration, agent and known hosts apply.

Secrets come from the stack's secret prefix:

  • <prefix><VAR> becomes /etc/<unit>/env.
  • <prefix>migrate/<VAR> reaches the migrate step only.
  • <prefix>files/<name> becomes /etc/<unit>/<name>.

They travel to the host on ssh's standard input, never on a command line or your disk.

These flags and variables apply to every deploy command:

Flag Meaning --ssh-key The hosts' SSH private key, used through the agent SSH_AUTH_SOCK names. Also DEPLOYFORGE_SSH_KEY. --operator Who is deploying, for the lock, the audit log and the ledger. Also DEPLOYFORGE_OPERATOR; defaults to $USER. --host-binary deployforge's linux/amd64 build, which runs on the host. Default bin/deployforge-linux-amd64. Also DEPLOYFORGE_HOST_BINARY. --health-timeout Seconds to wait for every host name to answer /readyz after a restart. Default 60. --keep Releases kept on the host, at least 2. Default 5. --ledger-dir Directory of the ledger files. Default deployments. --hooks Directory of hook scripts. Default .deployforge/hooks. --format text, or json for one JSON report on standard output from ship, release, rollback and status. See Reports. Default text.

AWS_PROFILE and AWS_REGION select the AWS profile and region when secrets are in SSM.

docs.title: deploy ship
docs.text:
ship is the routine deploy. It packages the app with its release script in a temporary git worktree, so your checkout is left alone. It deploys the archive as deploy release does, with the stack's config, and checks https://<host>/readyz for each of the stack's host names from outside.

deployforge deploy ship example-app prod --tag v1.2.0

The config defaults to stacks/<app>/<stack>/config.yaml; set --config for another. The release script defaults to ops/host/release.sh; set --script for another. The app's checkout defaults to $GOPATH/src/<repo>; set --repo for another.

With --tag, ship fetches the tag from origin and packages it with GOWORK off. --no-fetch skips the fetch.

The script receives the deployforge binary in DEPLOYFORGE and the fleet document in DEPLOYFORGE_FLEET. It builds the app for linux/amd64 and runs $DEPLOYFORGE release package. See Release package. A program that embeds the CLI can add environment for scripts at older tags that read other names, with Options.ReleaseEnv (see Embedding); release package also accepts --sites as an older name of --fleet.

The script must be executable in the commit being packaged, which is the mode git recorded (100755), not the mode in your checkout. ship reads it before running the script and stops when it is not, with the fix:

git update-index --chmod=+x ops/host/release.sh
git commit -m "fix(ops): make the release script executable"

Then tag again. A shell script beside it that is not executable is reported as a warning, since the release script may run it.

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
--dry-run packages and checks the release, then stops. Nothing is snapshotted, deployed or recorded:

deployforge deploy ship example-app prod --tag v1.2.0 --dry-run

docs.title: Local builds
docs.text:
--local packages a local commit, untagged, instead of a tag. --ref names the app's branch or commit; the default is main.

deployforge deploy ship example-app staging --local \
  --with github.com/example-org/example-lib \
  --with-web github.com/example-org/example-web@my-branch
  • --with <host/org/repo>[@ref] builds an upstream Go module from its local checkout ($GOPATH/src/<repo>, main unless @ref is given) through a generated go.work.
  • --with-web <host/org/repo>[@ref] builds and packs the repository's npm packages with pnpm, and installs them in place of the front end's own. This happens in the temporary worktree only.

The archive and the ledger name every upstream commit used. Every commit a local build uses must be on a remote branch. --allow-unpushed <repo> excuses a repository from that rule; repeat it for each.

docs.title: Snapshot before a primary stack
docs.text: Before it deploys an app's primary stack that has databases, ship takes a snapshot of the database server and waits until it is available. This applies when the server is a Lightsail database, which means the fleet document sets databaseServer.lightsailName. A migrate that goes wrong can then be undone by restoring the snapshot. A snapshot that fails stops the deploy. --no-db-snapshot skips it. See Databases.

docs.title: Credential pre-flight
docs.text: When the fleet document names a credential registry, ship first checks that every secret the registry stores under the stack's prefix is in the parameter store, by name. It stops before packaging if one is missing. --no-preflight skips it. See Credentials.

docs.title: Other ship flags
docs.text: Flag Meaning --selfcheck enforce, report or off: run the app's self-check, if the fleet document turns it on. Default report. --skip-public-check Do not check the host names from outside afterwards. --dry-run Package and check the release only; deploy nothing.

docs.title: deploy release
docs.text:
release takes an archive you already have. It checks the archive, ships it to the stack and records it in the ledger.

deployforge deploy release example-app prod \
  --archive dist/example-app-0123abc.tgz \
  --config stacks/example-app/prod/config.yaml \
  --tag v1.2.0

--sha256 gives the archive's checksum; by default deployforge reads the first field of <archive>.sha256. --selfcheck takes the same values as for ship.

docs.title: deploy rollback
docs.text:
deployforge deploy rollback example-app prod

Rollback switches the stack back to the release before the current one and records it in the ledger. The host must keep a second release. Rollback does not reverse migrations, so write migrations that the previous release can run with.

docs.title: deploy unlock
docs.text:
deployforge deploy unlock example-app prod

A deploy that is cut off can leave its lock behind. unlock removes it and changes nothing else. Check deploy status first to see who holds the lock.

docs.title: deploy status
docs.text:
deployforge deploy status example-app prod

status reads the host and changes nothing. It shows the release current points at, the release directories kept, who holds the deploy lock, and whether the host has deployforge's audit log. It compares the live release with the ledger's.

docs.title: deploy unpushed
docs.text:
deployforge deploy unpushed --fetch

unpushed reads each stack's live release from the ledger and checks the app's commit and every upstream input of a local build against the remote branches of its checkout under $GOPATH/src. It prints what is not pushed or cannot be checked, and exits non-zero if anything is. --fetch fetches each checkout's origin first.

docs.title: On-host steps
docs.text:
For one release, the host runs these steps in order:

  1. Lock. The lock file records who and when. It is created exclusively, so a second deploy fails.
  2. Unpack the archive as /opt/<unit>/releases/<id>. The id is <UTC timestamp>-<revision>.
  3. Install the config, the environment file and the key files under /etc/<unit>/. Each is written to a temporary name and renamed. The previous set is kept for restore.
  4. Validate: run the new binary's validate as the stack's user.
  5. Migrate: run the new binary's migrate as the stack's user, with the migrate-only variables in a temporary environment file removed afterwards.
  6. Switch: point /opt/<unit>/current at the new release and restart the unit.
  7. Readiness: wait for /readyz on the loopback port, once for each host name in the Host header, until --health-timeout.
  8. Restore: if any step fails, put back the previous release and files, restart, and check readiness again. The error names the step that failed. Completed migrations stay applied; see Migrations.
  9. Prune: keep the newest --keep releases, and always the live one and the one it replaced; remove the rest.
  10. Audit: write one JSON line for the action in the app's directory on the host, then unlock.

When the fleet document turns on selfcheck, the app's selfcheck subcommand runs before and after the switch, as --selfcheck says.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
A rollback, and the restore after a failed deploy, switch the code back. They never reverse a migration. The previous release then runs against the schema the new release migrated, so every migration must work with the release before it. Make each schema change in two releases, expand then contract:

  1. Expand. Add what the new code needs: a new table, or a column that is nullable or has a default. The old code ignores it. Write to both the old and new shapes where the code moves data across.
  2. Contract. Once no release you could roll back to uses the old shape, remove it in a later release.

A change that the previous release cannot run against is not safe to deploy unattended. That includes dropping or renaming a column or table it reads, adding a NOT NULL column without a default, or narrowing a type. Split it as above. If you can't, deploy it by hand, after ship has taken its snapshot, and plan to restore the snapshot instead of rolling back.

A failed deploy says whether its migration completed: the error, and failure.migrated in a report. When it did, the previous release is running on the migrated schema.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
With --format json, ship, release, rollback and status write one JSON document to standard output and send their progress to standard error. An agent or a script reads the report instead of the prose. The exit status still says whether the command failed.

{"command":"ship","app":"example-app","stack":"prod","ok":false,"phase":"deploy",
 "error":"…","failure":{"step":"health","kept":false,"restored":true,"migrated":true,"error":"…"},
 "snapshot":"example-app-prod-…"}
Field Meaning ok The command did all it set out to. phase Where it failed: preflight (checks before packaging), package, snapshot, deploy, public-check, or status. failure How the host's part failed, when it got that far. step is unpack, install, validate, selfcheck-pre, migrate, switch, health or selfcheck-post. kept means the running release was never switched away from. restored means the previous release and its files run again. stopped means a first release failed, so nothing runs. migrated means the release's migration completed and stays applied. entry The ledger entry recorded. A ship that failed its public-check has one: the release is live and recorded. snapshot The database snapshot ship took first. status, ledger For status: what the host reports, and the ledger's current release.

docs.title: The ledger
docs.text:
The ledger is a JSON Lines file for each stack in --dir (default deployments), kept in your repository. A successful deploy or rollback appends an entry. It never holds a secret value. Commit the file after each deploy.

deployforge ledger show example-app prod -n 5
deployforge ledger current example-app prod
  • ledger show <app> <stack> prints the most recent entries. -n sets how many; 0 prints all; the default is 10.
  • ledger current <app> <stack> prints the release the stack runs, and fails if it was never deployed.
  • ledger record appends an entry by hand, after checking it against the history. Its flags are --app, --stack, --action (deploy or rollback, default deploy), --release, --previous, --revision, --tag, --sha256 (required for a deploy), --time, --operator, --input and --selfcheck.
  • ledger import <app> <stack> --from <file> brings in a ledger written by another tool. See Taking over a stack.

Every ledger command takes --dir to name the ledger directory.

docs.title: Hooks
docs.text:
Hooks are executables in the hooks directory (.deployforge/hooks unless --hooks says otherwise). They run on your machine, named for the moment they run:

Hook Runs before-package Before packaging. after-package After packaging. before-deploy Before a release is deployed. after-deploy After a release is deployed and recorded. before-rollback Before a rollback. after-rollback After a rollback is done and recorded. failed After any of the above fails.

A hook that does not exist is skipped. A hook gets these environment variables, and never a secret value:

  • DEPLOYFORGE_HOOK, the hook's name
  • DEPLOYFORGE_APP
  • DEPLOYFORGE_STACK
  • DEPLOYFORGE_HOST
  • DEPLOYFORGE_OPERATOR
  • DEPLOYFORGE_RELEASE
  • DEPLOYFORGE_REVISION
  • DEPLOYFORGE_TAG
  • DEPLOYFORGE_ERROR, for failed

Failure rules:

  • A failing before- hook stops what it precedes.
  • An after- hook runs once the change is done and recorded. Its failure is reported but does not undo the change.
  • A failure of the failed hook is only logged.

The host steps run inside one request, so they have no hooks of their own.

docs.title: Deploy runbook
docs.text:
deployforge deploy runbook --app example-app --stack prod list
deployforge deploy runbook --app example-app --stack prod restart --note v1.2.3
DEPLOY_SOURCE=--tag=v1.2.3 deployforge deploy runbook --app example-app --stack prod run 2
deployforge deploy runbook --app example-app --stack prod doc --html -o deploy-example-app-prod.html

Each live stack has a recurring deploy runbook: one run per deploy, from the operator's shell to the recorded deploy. Its steps are:

  1. Prepare: the operator's shell (the SSH key in the agent, the AWS profile answering, the stack's unit on its host as host setup --check compares it, and, when the tool gives admin addresses and the host its lightsailName, the host's firewall as host ports checks it); the stack's secrets, with credentials preflight --record when the fleet names a registry; and a dry run.
  2. Deploy: deploy ship, with every host name checked from outside, then the deploy recorded: the stack's credentials marked deployed and the ledger committed.

DEPLOY_SOURCE holds what to deploy: --tag=v1.2.3, or --local for the pushed commit on main. Begin each deploy after the first with restart --note <release>; earlier runs stay in the event log, so state says when the stack was last deployed and whether it finished. run 2 runs the deploy phase in one go, and prepare 2 says what it still needs. The event log is deployments/runbooks/<app>-<stack>.events.json; export writes the runbook as JSON.

A tool embedding deployforge names its own command with Options.RunbookTool, and keeps the logs elsewhere with Options.RunbookDir. For its own runbooks, package runbookkit has remote quoting for ssh, install-from-console actions, permission lists, step needs derived from commands, inputs such as an SSH key in the agent or a session token, and fixes for the failures these runs meet.

docs.title: Release package
docs.text:
release package writes a reproducible archive and its .sha256 file. Your app's release script normally calls it:

deployforge release package example-app \
  --repo . --from build/ --out dist

It checks that:

  • the app's checkout is clean, is the repository the fleet document names, and has no replace directives;
  • the checkout is at a release tag;
  • the --from directory holds a static linux/amd64 binary named for the app, plus its web files.

Flags:

  • --repo: the app's checkout.
  • --from: the directory the app's build wrote.
  • --out: where to write the archive and checksum. Default dist.
  • --allow-untagged: package a revision with no release tag, for a trial or a local build.
  • --input <repo@commit>: an upstream commit the build took from a local commit. Repeat for each.

docs.title: Edge
docs.text:
This guide covers Cloudflare as the edge in front of your apps: checking DNS zones against their name servers, hardening zones through Cloudflare's API, checking the minimum TLS version, and issuing origin certificates. Set edge to cloudflare on an app to use it; see Fleet document. The host side, including the Caddyfile that serves the certificate, is in Hosts.

Commands that call Cloudflare read the API token from CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN. Zone commands read the zones document, zones.json by default. Use --zones <path> for another file.

docs.title: The zones document
docs.text:
zones.json lists every DNS zone the fleet owns. Print its schema with deployforge zones schema.

{
  "formatVersion": "1",
  "zones": [
    {
      "name": "example.com",
      "registrar": "example-registrar",
      "dns": "cloudflare",
      "records": [
        {
          "name": "app",
          "type": "A",
          "values": ["203.0.113.10"],
          "proxied": true,
          "purpose": "app",
          "source": "example-app/prod",
          "host": "web-1",
          "status": "present",
          "check": { "path": "/readyz", "status": 200 }
        }
      ],
      "hardening": {}
    }
  ]
}

Zone fields: name, registrar, dns (cloudflare or registrar), records, hardening and notes.

Record fields:

  • name: the label under the zone, or @ for the zone itself.
  • type: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT or WORKER.
  • values: the values. For a proxied record, the origin.
  • proxied: whether Cloudflare proxies the record.
  • purpose: static-site, app, redirect, mail, verification or parked.
  • source, host, notes: where it is served from, what serves it, and anything else to know.
  • status: present, or planned. verify skips planned records.
  • check: an HTTPS request to the host that must answer as given: path, status and an optional location prefix.

docs.title: Check zones
docs.text:
deployforge zones validate
deployforge zones verify
deployforge zones get https://app.example.com/readyz
deployforge zones page -o zones.md
  • zones validate checks the document, and that every live host name of the fleet has a record.
  • zones verify [zone...] asks each zone's name servers for every listed record and makes the records' HTTPS checks.
  • zones get <https-url> resolves the host at its zone's own name servers, as verify does, so a record added moments ago is reached even while a resolver caches its absence. It exits non-zero unless the answer has --status (default 200), and a Location starting with --location when you set it.
  • zones page writes a Markdown page of the zones document, to -o or standard output.
  • zones schema writes the zones document's JSON Schema, to -o or standard output.

verify has two flags for staged changes. --records-only checks the records but not their HTTPS checks, as before a planned change while a host is down. --fail-planned fails a planned record instead of skipping it, as after a step that adds records.

docs.title: Harden zones
docs.text:
zones harden sets each zone's TLS settings and writes its custom rules, rate limit, Free Managed Ruleset, cache rule and www redirect. The baseline is the same for every zone. Each zone's hardening section holds only what differs. The rules carry refs beginning with fleet-; other rules in a phase are kept.

deployforge zones harden plan
deployforge zones harden apply --confirm
deployforge zones harden verify
  • plan [zone...] says what differs from the baseline and what apply would do. It changes nothing.
  • apply [zone...] --confirm changes what differs, then verifies. It needs --confirm.
  • verify [zone...] checks every zone matches and exits non-zero if not.

Name zones to act on them, or leave them out for every zone with hardening. The token needs Zone Read, Zone Settings Edit, Zone WAF Edit, Cache Rules Edit, Single Redirect Edit and Bot Management Edit. Zone Read is enough for plan and verify.

docs.title: The hardening section
docs.text:
{
  "hardening": {
    "allowCountries": ["US", "CA"],
    "countryHosts": ["app", "auth"],
    "botFightModeOff": true,
    "wwwRedirect": true,
    "rateLimit": { "path": "/login-token", "requests": 5, "whenRecord": "auth" },
    "noCachePrefixes": ["/api/"]
  }
}
  • allowCountries and countryHosts: the only countries allowed (ISO 3166-1 alpha-2) on the listed labels under the zone.
  • botFightModeOff: turn Bot Fight Mode off.
  • wwwRedirect: redirect www to the apex with a 301, keeping the path and query.
  • rateLimit: limit one exact path per client address. requests is how many one address may make in 10 seconds; the default is 5. whenRecord names a record label that must exist before the limit applies.
  • noCachePrefixes: path prefixes never cached, besides / and .html documents.

docs.title: Check the minimum TLS version
docs.text:
deployforge zones tls
deployforge zones tls app.example.com

zones tls [<host>...] checks from outside that each host refuses TLS 1.1 and accepts TLS 1.2. With no host it checks every live stack's host names.

docs.title: Origin certificates
docs.text:
An app behind Cloudflare serves a Cloudflare Origin CA certificate for its zone and *.zone. The key is made on the host and never leaves it.

deployforge origin-cert install example.com web-1
deployforge caddy install web-1
  • origin-cert install <zone> <host> makes a key and CSR on the host with openssl, has Cloudflare sign it, and installs the certificate and key as /etc/caddy/certs/<zone>.pem and .key, owned by root:caddy, mode 0640. Reload Caddy to serve it. --ssh-key names the host's key.
  • origin-cert issue <zone> reads a PEM CSR on standard input and writes the signed certificate to -o or standard output. Its ID and expiry go to standard error. --days sets the validity: 7, 30, 90, 365, 730, 1095 or 5475 (the default, fifteen years).
  • origin-cert list <zone> lists the zone's certificates: ID, expiry and host names.
  • origin-cert revoke <id> --confirm revokes a certificate. Cloudflare then refuses an origin that still serves it, so revoke a certificate you replaced only once nothing serves it.

An example of issue with a CSR you made elsewhere:

deployforge origin-cert issue example.com --days 365 -o example.com.pem < example.com.csr

docs.title: Cloudflare's ranges
docs.text:
Caddy and the host's firewall trust Cloudflare's proxy ranges, which deployforge carries in deploy/cfranges/ips-v4.txt and ips-v6.txt. Cloudflare changes them rarely.

deployforge cloudflare-ips --check
deployforge cloudflare-ips --dir deploy/cfranges
  • cloudflare-ips --check compares the ranges this build carries with the lists Cloudflare publishes, and fails when Cloudflare has added or removed one. Run it in a scheduled job.
  • cloudflare-ips writes the published lists to --dir (default deploy/cfranges), for review and a release of deployforge.

docs.title: Embedding
docs.text: This guide is for Go developers who want deployforge inside their own tools. deployforge is library first: each capability is a package with no command-line code, and the deployforge command is a thin layer over them. You can import the packages, or mount the whole command tree under your own command and add commands beside it. See Getting started for the command line, and Deploying for what the commands do.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Each capability lives in its own package. The cli package holds the Cobra command tree.
  • Every CDN or cloud API sits behind an interface in the package that uses it. Cloudflare and AWS implementations live in subpackages, so tests use fakes and another provider can be added without touching the callers.
  • The host side of a deploy is the same binary, run as root over SSH with a JSON request on standard input. There is no agent on the host.

docs.title: Packages
Mount the command tree
docs.text:
cli.New returns the root *cobra.Command. The deployforge command is just this:

err := cli.New(cli.Options{}).ExecuteContext(ctx)

To mount it under your own tool, rename it with Use and add it as a subcommand:

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "os"

    "github.com/spf13/cobra"

    "github.com/plexusone/deployforge/cli"
)

func main() {
    root := &cobra.Command{Use: "mytool"}
    root.AddCommand(cli.New(cli.Options{
        Use:   "deploy-fleet",
        Fleet: "ops/fleet.json",
    }))
    // Add your own commands beside it.
    if err := root.Execute(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The tree sets SilenceUsage and SilenceErrors, so print the returned error yourself, as the deployforge command does.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Every field is optional. A nil function uses the default, which is the real service.

Field Meaning Use The root command's name. deployforge when empty. Fleet The fleet document's default path. fleet.json when empty. The --fleet flag still overrides it. Store Opens the secret store a release reads. AWS SSM Parameter Store with the default AWS configuration when nil. Dial Reaches hosts with an SSH key. The system's ssh and scp when nil. Params Opens the parameter store that database provisioning reads and writes. AWS SSM Parameter Store when nil. Lightsail Opens the client database snapshots use. Lightsail with the default AWS configuration when nil. OriginCA Opens Cloudflare's Origin CA. The official client, with the token in CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, when nil. IAM Opens the clients the iam command uses. IAM and STS with the default AWS configuration when nil. CredentialConnector Reaches the credential stores for the check before a deploy. credforge's, through the targets, when nil. ReleaseEnv Extra environment for an app's release script, as NAME=value, from the running binary's path and the fleet document's. For scripts at older tags that read other names for them. None when nil. ImportHook Adds a host tool's own flags and replacements to db import, such as an ID it looks up in the target database once the owner's connection and the host are known. None when nil. HostPorts Opens the client host ports reads a firewall with. Lightsail with the default AWS configuration when nil. AdminCIDRs The addresses SSH should be open to: host ports' default for --admin-cidr, and the firewall check in each stack's deploy runbook. None when empty. RunbookTool How a deploy runbook's commands run the tool, such as a host tool's binary and its fleet flag. This program with --fleet when empty. RunbookDir Where each stack's deploy runbook event log is kept. deployments/runbooks when empty.

Their types are:

Store               func(c *cobra.Command) (secrets.Store, error)
Dial                func(key string) deployer.Dialer
Params              func(c *cobra.Command) (dbroles.Store, error)
Lightsail           func(c *cobra.Command) (dbsnapshot.API, error)
OriginCA            func() (origincert.API, error)
IAM                 func(c *cobra.Command) (stackiam.Clients, error)
CredentialConnector func(*targets.File) credforge.Connector
ReleaseEnv          func(self, fleet string) []string
ImportHook          func(cmd *cobra.Command) cli.ImportReplacer
HostPorts           func(c *cobra.Command) (hostports.API, error)
AdminCIDRs          []string
RunbookTool         []string
RunbookDir          string

An ImportReplacer receives the database's owner connection and a runner for commands on the via host, and returns the replacements to apply:

type ImportReplacer func(ctx context.Context, dsn string, r dbimport.Remote, out io.Writer) ([]dbimport.Replacement, error)

Replace a field to use another secret store or transport, or to test your tool with fakes.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: The cli package exports the names of the variables the commands read: EnvSSHKey (DEPLOYFORGE_SSH_KEY), EnvOperator (DEPLOYFORGE_OPERATOR) and EnvHostBinary (DEPLOYFORGE_HOST_BINARY).

docs.title: Fleet document
docs.text: This guide describes every part of the fleet document, fleet.json: hosts, apps, stacks, the database server and the credentials section. deployforge refuses unknown keys, so a misspelled field is an error. Run deployforge schema to print the JSON Schema the document follows, and deployforge validate to check a document. See Getting started for a minimal example, Hosts for what the host fields drive, and Databases and Credentials for the sections they use.

docs.title: Top level
docs.text:
Field Meaning $schema The JSON Schema the file follows, for editors. formatVersion Required. Must be "1". portRange Required. min and max, within 1024 to 65535. Stack ports come from here. hosts Required. The machines apps run on. At least one. primaryStack The stack named for the app alone. prod when empty. acmeEmail The address Caddy registers with for certificates it gets itself, for apps with no edge. apps The deployed apps. databaseServer The PostgreSQL server, when deployforge provisions roles. credentials The credential registry.

The primary stack decides names. The unit and Unix user of the primary stack are named for the app: example-app. Any other stack's unit is <app>-<stack>, such as example-app-staging. The Unix user is the unit name without hyphens and must be at most 32 characters.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text:
{ "name": "web-1", "address": "203.0.113.10", "sshUser": "ubuntu" }
  • name: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Stacks refer to the host by this name.
  • address: the address for SSH.
  • addressFrom: read the address from a Pulumi output instead. Give address or addressFrom, not both.
  • sshUser: the user to connect as, with sudo. ubuntu when empty.
  • lightsailName: the host's name as a Lightsail instance, for host ports to read its firewall.
{
  "name": "web-1",
  "addressFrom": { "pulumi": { "dir": "stack", "stack": "prod", "output": "staticIp" } }
}

dir is the Pulumi project's directory. deployforge runs pulumi stack output when it needs the address, so the document holds no IP. See Hosts.

docs.title: Apps
docs.text:
{
  "name": "example-app",
  "repo": "github.com/example-org/example-app",
  "domain": "example.com",
  "edge": "cloudflare",
  "secretPrefix": "/example/{stack}/example-app/",
  "stateDirectory": false,
  "selfcheck": false,
  "logFiles": ["security.jsonl"],
  "labels": { "owner": "example-org" },
  "notes": "Why the app is set up this way.",
  "stacks": {}
}
Field Meaning name The app's name: its binary, and with the stack, its unit, user and paths. repo The repository that builds the binary, as <host>/<owner>/<repo>. domain The DNS zone every host name of the app is in. Each stack host name must be the domain or end in .<domain>. edge cloudflare, or empty for none. With cloudflare, Caddy serves the zone's origin certificate and trusts Cloudflare's addresses to name the client. With none, Caddy gets its own certificates. An app behind cloudflare needs domain, and each of its host names must be the domain or one label under it, such as app.example.com: the zone's certificates cover only the zone and *.zone. secretPrefix Where the app's secrets are in the parameter store. Starts and ends with / and contains {stack}. stateDirectory The app keeps state on local disk, so its unit gets a private writable state directory. selfcheck A deploy runs the app's selfcheck subcommand before and after the switch. See Deploying. logFiles Files the app writes under /var/log/<unit>/. The host rotates them daily by rename and keeps a week. Plain file names only. labels String facts deployforge keeps but never acts on, for tools around it. notes Why the app is set up this way. JSON has no comments. stacks The app's deployments by name. At least one.

docs.title: Stacks
docs.text:
{
  "host": "web-1",
  "hosts": ["app.example.com", "auth.example.com"],
  "loopbackHosts": ["auth.example.com"],
  "port": 8101,
  "databases": [
    { "name": "example_auth" },
    { "name": "example", "appRole": true, "appDsn": "EXAMPLE_PG_DSN" }
  ],
  "status": "live",
  "limits": { "memoryMax": "512M", "cpuQuota": "50%", "connectionLimit": 10 }
}
Field Meaning host The host the stack runs on, by name. hosts Host names the reverse proxy forwards to the stack. At least one. Each name is used by one stack only. loopbackHosts Names among hosts that the host resolves to itself, so the app's calls to them stay on the host. port The loopback port. Inside portRange and unused on its host. deployforge next-port <host> prints a free one. databases The stack's databases. See below. status planned, live or elsewhere. limits Required once the stack is live.

Status means:

  • planned: not deployed yet.
  • live: runs on its host and is deployed by deployforge.
  • elsewhere: runs outside the fleet until it moves in. Databases describes how roles for such a stack are staged.

Limits:

  • memoryMax: systemd MemoryMax, such as 512M or 1G.
  • cpuQuota: systemd CPUQuota, such as 50%.
  • connectionLimit: each database role's CONNECTION LIMIT. Match your app's pool size to it.

docs.title: Databases
docs.text:
Each database has an owner role <name>_owner, which migrates it. With appRole set, the app runs as a separate role <name>_app with rows only. Otherwise it runs as the owner. Database names are lowercase letters, digits and underscores, and each name is unique across the fleet.

Field Meaning name The database's name. appRole The app runs as a separate role. ownerDsn The parameter, under the secret prefix, holding the owner's connection string, such as migrate/EXAMPLE_PG_ADMIN_DSN. appDsn The parameter holding the app role's connection string. appPassword A parameter holding the app role's password alone, for a migration that sets it.

appDsn and appPassword need appRole. A parameter under migrate/ reaches only the migrate step.

docs.title: Database server
docs.text:
{
  "databaseServer": {
    "endpoint": "db.example.com",
    "port": 5432,
    "adminUser": "admin",
    "adminDatabase": "fleet",
    "adminPassword": { "parameter": "/example/admin/password" },
    "via": "web-1",
    "lockdown": ["fleet"],
    "reachable": ["template1"],
    "lightsailName": "example-pg"
  }
}
Field Meaning endpoint The server's host name. endpointFrom Read the endpoint from a Pulumi output, as for a host address. Give endpoint or endpointFrom. port 5432 when empty. adminUser, adminDatabase The administrator provisioning connects as, and its database. adminPassword Where the password is kept. Give exactly one of parameter (a full name starting with /) or pulumiConfig (dir, stack, key). via The fleet host that runs psql against the server. The operator's machine need not reach it. lockdown The server's other databases, which no app's role may reach. reachable Databases the provider owns whose CONNECT cannot be revoked, such as template1. lightsailName The server's name as a Lightsail database. Without it, no snapshots are taken.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
{
  "credentials": {
    "registry": "credentials/registry.json",
    "events": "credentials/events.json",
    "reviews": "credentials/reviews.json",
    "targets": "credentials/targets.json"
  }
}

Only registry is required. Every path is relative to the fleet document. events and reviews default to events.json and reviews.json beside the registry. targets is a credforge targets file. See Credentials.

docs.title: What validate checks
docs.text: validate reports every problem at once. Among them: an unknown format version, a bad port range, a name, unit, host name or database used twice, a stack on an unknown host, a port outside the range or used on its host, a host name outside the app's domain, a secret prefix without {stack}, and a live stack without limits.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text:
deployforge fleet inventory -o docs/inventory.md
deployforge fleet format -o docs/fleet-format.md

fleet inventory writes a Markdown page of the fleet: each app's stacks with their host, host names, port, databases and status; each app's secret prefix, edge and labels; each stack's unit, Unix user and limits; and the apps' notes. fleet format writes this document's format reference from the Go types the schema is generated from, so it cannot drift. Commit both, and write them again when the fleet or deployforge changes.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This guide takes you from nothing to a first deploy: installing deployforge, writing a minimal fleet document, checking it, preparing a host, and shipping a release. For every field of the fleet document, see Fleet document. For what a deploy does, see Deploying. For host preparation in detail, see Hosts.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: go install github.com/plexusone/deployforge/cmd/deployforge@latest

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Linux host with systemd and Caddy 2. host setup and caddy install prepare the rest.
  • SSH access to the host as a user with sudo. The default user is ubuntu; set sshUser on the host to change it.
  • A parameter store for secrets. deployforge reads them from AWS SSM Parameter Store, using your AWS profile and region (AWS_PROFILE, AWS_REGION).
  • An app repository with a release script (ops/host/release.sh by default) that builds the app for linux/amd64 and calls release package.
  • A linux/amd64 build of deployforge for the host. It runs there during a deploy. Pass it with --host-binary or DEPLOYFORGE_HOST_BINARY.

docs.title: A minimal fleet document
docs.text:
Save this as fleet.json in your operations repository:

{
  "formatVersion": "1",
  "portRange": { "min": 8101, "max": 8199 },
  "hosts": [{ "name": "web-1", "address": "203.0.113.10" }],
  "apps": [
    {
      "name": "example-app",
      "repo": "github.com/example-org/example-app",
      "domain": "example.com",
      "secretPrefix": "/example/{stack}/example-app/",
      "stacks": {
        "prod": {
          "host": "web-1",
          "hosts": ["app.example.com"],
          "port": 8101,
          "status": "live",
          "limits": { "memoryMax": "512M", "cpuQuota": "50%", "connectionLimit": 10 }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

A live stack needs limits. The app gets certificates from Caddy itself, because it names no edge. Set acmeEmail at the top level to give Caddy an address to register with.

Print the schema to get completion in your editor:

deployforge schema > fleet.schema.json

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
deployforge validate

validate reports every problem it finds. On success it prints the counts of hosts, apps and stacks. Commands read fleet.json in the current directory. Use --fleet <path> for another file.

docs.title: Prepare the host
docs.text:
Run these once for each stack, and again when the host layout changes:

deployforge host setup example-app prod --apply
deployforge caddy install web-1

host setup creates the stack's Unix user, its /opt and /etc directories, its systemd unit, log rotation, and /etc/hosts lines for loopback host names. It never starts the service. Without --apply it prints the script, so you can read it first.

caddy install renders the host's Caddyfile, has Caddy validate it on the host, keeps the old file, and reloads Caddy.

Your parameters must exist before the first deploy. A parameter named <prefix><VAR> becomes an environment variable, so /example/prod/example-app/SESSION_KEY becomes SESSION_KEY in /etc/example-app/env.

docs.title: First deploy
docs.text:
Put the stack's config at stacks/example-app/prod/config.yaml. deployforge installs it as is. Tag the app and push the tag, then ship it:

deployforge deploy ship example-app prod --tag v1.0.0 \
  --host-binary bin/deployforge-linux-amd64

ship packages the tag in a temporary worktree, deploys it, and checks https://<host>/readyz for each host name from outside. Commit the ledger entry it writes under deployments/.

Check the result:

deployforge ledger show example-app prod
deployforge deploy status example-app prod

To go back to the previous release, run deployforge deploy rollback example-app prod.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Fleet document: every field.
  • Deploying: local builds, rollback, hooks and the ledger.
  • Edge: Cloudflare zones and origin certificates.
  • Databases: roles, snapshots and copies.
  • Credentials: the credential registry and the pre-flight check.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text: This guide covers preparing a host for a stack and its reverse proxy: host setup, unit, caddyfile, caddy install, next-port, and addresses read from Pulumi outputs. The fields these commands read are in Fleet document. Once a host is ready, see Deploying. For certificates behind Cloudflare, see Edge.

docs.title: Print a unit
docs.text:
deployforge unit example-app prod

unit prints the stack's systemd unit, with its hardening sandbox and the limits from the fleet document. Use it to review what host setup will install.

docs.title: Set up a stack's place on its host
docs.text:
deployforge host setup example-app prod            # print the script
deployforge host setup example-app prod --apply    # run it on the host
deployforge host setup example-app prod --check    # compare the host's unit, changing nothing

The script makes the stack's Unix user, its /opt and /etc directories, its systemd unit, the rotation of its log files, and the /etc/hosts lines for its loopback host names. It is idempotent, so you can run it again. It never starts the service, because a stack has no release to run until its first deploy.

--apply runs the script on the stack's host over SSH, with sudo. --ssh-key names the host's SSH private key, used through the agent SSH_AUTH_SOCK names.

--check reads the unit installed on the host and compares it with the one the fleet document gives, comments and blank lines aside. It exits non-zero, naming the first line that differs, when they do not match, such as after a change to the stack's limits, and when the host has no unit yet. It changes nothing. Install the new unit with --apply; the next deploy restarts the service under it. Each stack's deploy runbook runs --check before it ships.

docs.title: Find a free port
docs.text:
deployforge next-port web-1

next-port prints the lowest port in portRange that no stack on the host uses. It fails when the range is full.

docs.title: Caddyfile
docs.text:
deployforge caddyfile web-1

caddyfile prints the host's Caddyfile, with one block per live stack on it. To include a stack that is not live yet, add --with:

deployforge caddyfile web-1 --with example-app/staging

Name each stack as app/stack, and repeat --with for each.

With edge set to cloudflare, the blocks use the zone's origin certificate and trust Cloudflare's addresses to name the client. With no edge, Caddy gets its own certificates, registered with acmeEmail.

docs.title: Install the Caddyfile
docs.text:
deployforge caddy install web-1

caddy install renders the Caddyfile, uploads it, and has Caddy validate it on the host before anything is replaced. It keeps the running one as /etc/caddy/Caddyfile.previous, installs the new one and reloads Caddy. It never restarts Caddy, so the other apps keep serving.

To go back, copy the previous file over the Caddyfile and reload Caddy.

Flags: --with as above, and --ssh-key.

docs.title: Addresses from Pulumi outputs
docs.text:
A host can take its address from a Pulumi stack output, so the fleet document holds no IP:

{
  "name": "web-1",
  "addressFrom": { "pulumi": { "dir": "stack", "stack": "prod", "output": "staticIp" } }
}

Every command that reaches the host resolves the address when it needs it, by running pulumi stack output in dir. pulumi must be installed and logged in. The same form, endpointFrom, works for the database server's endpoint. The database administrator's password can come from a Pulumi secret with adminPassword.pulumiConfig. See Databases.

docs.title: Check a host's firewall
docs.text:
deployforge host ports web-1 --admin-cidr 192.0.2.10/32 --admin-cidr 198.51.100.7/32

host ports <host> reads the Lightsail instance's port states, the host's lightsailName in the fleet document, and exits non-zero unless:

  • HTTPS (443) is open exactly to Cloudflare's IPv4 ranges, and with --ipv6 its IPv6 ranges too;
  • SSH (22) is open only to the --admin-cidr addresses;
  • no other port is open.

It reports each range missing or extra, and changes nothing. A tool embedding deployforge can give the admin addresses once, with Options.AdminCIDRs, so host ports <host> needs no flags. Run it after any change to the firewall; each stack's deploy runbook also runs it before a ship (see Deploying). Lightsail replaces an instance's rules as a whole, and a tool that replaces them new-first, then deletes the old set, can close the ports it just opened: every site behind the host then times out while the host itself is healthy.

docs.title: Taking over a stack
docs.text: This guide moves a stack that another tool deployed into deployforge, without a redeploy. It works when the other tool used the same layout on the host: /opt/<unit>/releases, a current link and /etc/<unit>/. You bring in its ledger, check that the host and the ledger agree, and deploy. For the commands used afterwards, see Deploying. For the fleet entry the stack needs, see Fleet document.

docs.title: 1. Describe the stack
docs.text: Add the app and stack to the fleet document, with the same host, port and host names the running stack uses, and run deployforge validate.

docs.title: 2. Import the ledger
docs.text:
The old tool must have kept a JSON Lines ledger of the same entries. Import it:

deployforge ledger import example-app prod \
  --from old/example-app.jsonl --app-field site

--app-field names the field that holds the app when it is not called app. The default is app. import renames that field, checks every entry as ledger record checks it, in order, and writes nothing unless all pass. The stack's ledger must be empty, or be the file imported, which is replaced. The ledger lands in --dir, default deployments.

docs.title: 3. Compare the host with the ledger
docs.text:
deployforge deploy status example-app prod

status reads the host and changes nothing. It compares the live release with the ledger's. They must agree. A rollback also needs a second release kept on the host.

If they do not agree, fix the ledger or the host before you go on.

docs.title: 4. Deploy
docs.text:
deployforge deploy ship example-app prod --tag v1.2.3

The first deploy takes the deploy lock and starts deployforge's audit log on the host.

docs.title: The lock caveat
docs.text: The other tool takes no deploy lock. deployforge's lock protects only deploys made with deployforge. Once a stack has moved, deploy it only with deployforge, and stop using the old tool for that stack.

docs.title: PLAN: deployforge
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-DEPLOYFORGE-001 Status: proposed

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
deployforge starts from a working deploy engine rather than a blank page: the packages, their tests and their behavior come from a tool already used for production deploys, generalized where it assumed a particular fleet. Each phase ends with a release a team can use.

Phase Delivers Release 1. Deploy a release Fleet document, release packaging, secrets, the on-host switch with health and restore, ledger, lock and audit v0.1.0 2. The host around the apps Units, host setup, Caddy, ports v0.2.0 3. The edge Zones, hardening, origin certificates, edge workers v0.3.0 4. Databases Roles with connection limits, snapshots v0.4.0

docs.title: Order of Work
docs.text:
1. Types and schema first. The fleet document's Go types, validation and generated schema, with named stacks and per-stack databases.
  2. Move packages with their tests, one at a time, each building and passing before the next: release, provenance, ledger, deploy/target, deploy/archive, deploy/secrets, deploy/onhost, deploy/deployer.
  3. Add what was missing: the lock, the audit log, hooks, and the secrets Store interface.
  4. The command tree, mountable, with validate, schema, release package, deploy ship|release|rollback|unlock and ledger.
  5. A sample app in examples/ that deploys end to end against a disposable VM.

Phases 2 to 4 repeat the pattern for their packages.

docs.title: Design Decisions
docs.text:
• Binaries, not containers. A Go app is one static file; a registry and a runtime add cost and moving parts without adding safety.
  • Build on the operator's machine or CI, never on the server. The server runs only what was built from a pushed, tagged commit.
  • Health-gated switch with automatic restore, built in, not a hook.
  • Secrets stay in the parameter store and travel only inside the request to the host.
  • No agent on the host. The same binary runs there on demand, so there is nothing to keep running or patch.
  • Config is data with a schema. Anything that was compiled in for one fleet, such as database names, port ranges or a hardening baseline, becomes a field.
  • The CDN is optional, behind interfaces, Cloudflare first.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Generalizing breaks behavior a fleet relies on Packages move with their tests; a fleet already deployed by the engine is moved last, after a sample app runs end to end Rollback after an incompatible migration Documented expand-then-contract rule; a snapshot before a primary stack's deploy; a failed deploy reports whether its migration completed Root on the host The on-host command accepts only a typed request, validates every path under the app's directories, and runs nothing from the release before validate as the app's user Provider lock-in Interfaces per provider, with fakes in tests

docs.title: PRD: deployforge — ship Go apps to your own servers
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-DEPLOYFORGE-001 Status: proposed

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
A small team running a few Go web apps often wants them on one or two virtual machines it controls, not on a platform: each app a single static binary with a YAML config, run by systemd, behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS, with a CDN and firewall in front and a managed PostgreSQL behind. It is cheap, fast and easy to reason about.

The deploy itself is where it goes wrong. It starts as a shell script and grows until it is the riskiest code the team owns:

  • A release is built from a dirty checkout, or from a commit nobody pushed, and nobody can say later which code is running.
  • Secrets are copied by hand into an env file on the server, or into the script, and drift from where they are meant to live.
  • The new binary is started before its database migration ran, or the migration ran and the binary failed to start, and there is no clean way back.
  • A restart that fails its health check leaves the site down until someone notices.
  • Adding a second app to the same host means editing the proxy's config by hand, picking a free port, and hoping two apps never collide.
  • Each team writes this again, privately, because the tools that exist assume containers (and a registry), or build on the server from git, or have no health gate.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
deployforge deploys Go apps as release archives to hosts the team already has, safely and repeatably, from config files the team keeps in its own repository. One public binary does the work; the private repository holds only configuration, secrets' locations and the team's own runbooks.

A deploy is: build a release from a clean tagged commit, ship it with the app's config and its secrets, validate and migrate, switch, check health, and roll back on failure, recording what was deployed. deployforge also renders what the host needs around the apps (systemd units, the reverse proxy's config, host setup) and, optionally, the CDN in front of them.

docs.title: Users
docs.text:
• An operator of a few apps on one or more hosts, who wants one command per deploy and a record of every release.
  • A coding agent working for that operator: it prepares config, runs plans and checks, and reads the ledger, while the operator approves what cannot be undone.
  • A host tool that embeds deployforge's packages and commands, adding its own commands beside them.

docs.title: Phase 1: Deploy a release
docs.text:
1. Config files, not code. A fleet document lists the hosts, the apps, each app's stacks (such as prod and staging), their host names, ports, databases, resource limits and secret prefix. A JSON Schema is generated from the Go types, and deployforge validate checks the document: ports unique per host, host names unique, every required field set.
  2. Releases from a clean, tagged commit. release package refuses a dirty checkout, a replace directive, a revision that is not the tag's, or an unpushed commit, and writes an archive with its revision and checksum. A release can also be packaged by the app's own script, which calls release package.
  3. Secrets from a parameter store, never from the command line. A stack's secrets are read at deploy time from its prefix: variables under the prefix become the unit's environment file, variables under migrate/ reach only the migrate step, and parameters under files/ become files in the unit's config directory. No value is printed or logged. AWS SSM Parameter Store first; other stores through a provider interface.
  4. A safe switch. On the host, the release is unpacked into releases/<id>; the config and secrets are installed with the previous ones kept; the app's validate and migrate run as the app's user; the current symlink switches atomically and the unit restarts; the deploy waits for the app's readiness endpoint on each of its host names. Any failure restores the previous release and config. Old releases are pruned to a count.
  5. One command per deploy. deploy ship <app> <stack> --tag vX.Y.Z packages the release, optionally snapshots the database, deploys, and checks readiness through the public host names. deploy rollback switches back to the previous release.
  6. A ledger. Every deploy appends who, when, which revision and which release to a JSON Lines file per app, kept in the operator's repository.
  7. Locks and an audit trail. A deploy takes a lock on the host, so two cannot overlap; the host keeps an audit log of deploys and rollbacks.

docs.title: Phase 2: The host around the apps
docs.text:
1. systemd units rendered per app stack: user, directories, sandboxing, resource limits, an environment file, validate before start.
  2. Host setup as an idempotent script per app stack: the user, the directories, the unit, log rotation.
  3. Reverse proxy: Caddy's config rendered from the fleet document, one site block per app host, with origin certificates and the CDN's address ranges as trusted proxies; validated on the host before it replaces the running config, then reloaded, never restarted.
  4. Ports allocated from a configurable range, with next-port.

docs.title: Phase 3: The edge (optional)
docs.text:
1. DNS zones as a document: records checked against the CDN's API, with planned records that a step makes real.
  2. Hardening: a baseline of TLS settings, firewall rules and rate limits applied per zone from config, with plan, apply and verify.
  3. Origin certificates: a key made on the host, a CSR signed by the CDN, the certificate installed beside the key, with no key leaving the host.
  4. Static sites on the CDN's edge workers, deployed from a tagged commit and recorded like app releases.

Cloudflare first; each is optional, and a fleet without a CDN still deploys.

docs.title: Phase 4: Databases
docs.text:
1. Roles per app: an owner role that migrates and an app role that runs, each with a connection limit, their passwords generated into the parameter store and set on the server as SCRAM verifiers.
  2. Snapshots before a prod deploy, and on demand.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Containers, image registries or a container runtime.
  • Building on the server.
  • Provisioning the hosts or the database server; a separate tool (such as Pulumi) makes them, and deployforge reads their addresses.
  • Orchestrating many hosts per app, autoscaling or blue/green across machines in the first release.
  • Holding secret values in config files or in deployforge's own state.

docs.title: Success Measures
docs.text:
• A team moves an existing app to deployforge by writing config only.
  • A failed deploy leaves the previous release serving, every time, without a person stepping in.
  • Every running release can be traced from the ledger to a pushed, tagged commit.
  • No secret value appears in any file in the operator's repository, in any log, or on the command line.
